implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core ships the context object: HttpContext is created per request and carries Request, Response, User and the untyped Items bag, and middleware, controllers and Minimal API handlers receive it directly or inject IHttpContextAccessor (registered with AddHttpContextAccessor) when they cannot take it as a parameter. This replaces the classic context-object-plus-factory structure with a framework-owned per-request object; it is not thread-safe and must not outlive the request, so background work should copy the values it needs before the response is written.
pitfalls: HttpContext is not thread-safe; reading it from background work or parallel tasks can throw NullReferenceException once the request has completed.
IHttpContextAccessor returns null outside a request (startup, hosted services, timers), so the same service works in a request and fails silently elsewhere.

variants.name: AsyncLocal<T> ambient request state
variants.idiom_name: AsyncLocal<T> written at the request boundary
variants.implementation_notes: AsyncLocal<T> flows a value down an asynchronous control flow, which is what lets a service read request state without receiving it as a parameter; it is declared once (typically static) and assigned at the start of the request. Writes inside a child flow do not propagate back to the parent, so the value should be treated as immutable per request - the same ExecutionContext mechanism underlies the framework's own Activity/diagnostic flow.
pitfalls: A value assigned inside a child task or async scope is invisible to the parent flow, so 'set it deeper' designs silently no-op.
The value persists for as long as the ExecutionContext is alive: in long-running hosts (timers, message pumps) stale state stays visible unless every boundary reassigns it.
